title: Mussar begins
hookLine: Rabbi Israel Salanter starts a movement of ethical self-work

cards: The story starts with a boot. A shoemaker is mending it late at night, by a candle that has almost burned down, when a rabbi passing in the street stops at his door and asks why he's still at it.
The shoemaker shrugs: as long as the candle is burning, there's still time to mend. Tradition says the rabbi walked away repeating it to himself, like a verse.
The rabbi was Israel Salanter, and that is the heart of what he started.

teach.b: Rabbi Israel Salanter came out of the Lithuanian world of learning we've been visiting, the world of the Vilna Gaon and the yeshiva. He looked at people who knew the law brilliantly and asked an awkward question.
Knowing what is right is one thing. Becoming someone who does it, when you're tired, irritated, tempted, is another. So he urged people to study mussar.
The word appears in Proverbs, where the King James Bible renders it as instruction: "My son, hear the instruction of thy father." For Salanter, mussar meant teaching aimed at your own character.

He encouraged people to set aside time, alone or together in a room set apart for it, to read ethical works slowly and with feeling, often saying a single line aloud over and over until it sank from the mind into the heart.
Not to collect knowledge. To change. The Hebrew name for a trait of character is middah, a measure: patience, honesty, humility, anger, generosity.
Mussar works on one middah at a time, the way a craftsman fixes one seam, then the next.

teach.h: WHILE THE CANDLE BURNS, YOU CAN MEND.
teach.b: And it is honest about how slow that is. In the Mishnah, in Pirkei Avot, Hillel warns people not to trust in themselves until the day they die.
That sounds grim, but in mussar it is closer to hopeful: the work is never finished, so it's never too late to start.
Salanter's students carried this into the yeshivas, and some of those yeshivas made mussar study part of every day.

how: People who practice mussar today often study a classic ethical text in a small group or with a partner, choose one middah to focus on for a stretch of weeks, and keep a short journal of how it went.

games.q: you're Israel Salanter, surrounded by people who know the law brilliantly but don't always live it. what do you ask of them?
o: to study even more law, faster.
to set aside time to work on their own character, slowly and with feeling.
to stop studying and only do good deeds.
games.why: he urged mussar study: ethical works read slowly, lines repeated aloud, one trait at a time.

practice: Ask yourself, without judging, which one middah, one habit of the heart, has been costing you lately: impatience, sharpness with someone you love, putting things off.
Give it a short phrase in your own words, like "slow down before I answer," and repeat it quietly, the way Salanter's students repeated a line, until it feels less like an idea and more like a habit.

wordCard.voice: Mussar. Ethical instruction aimed at your own character, studied slowly, one trait at a time, the movement Rabbi Israel Salanter began. Today's word.
